opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that framing really sits at the center of almost every decision we make. Most AI products today are built around the chat paradigm: you ask a question, you get an answer in a few seconds, and the value is delivered in that single exchange. Research doesn't look like that. Real research is hours, days, sometimes weeks of work. You form a hypothesis, you gather evidence, you hit dead ends, you revise, and you build up context that has to persist across all of it. So if you take seriously that research is a long-horizon task, a lot of the standard assumptions break.

On pricing, the per-seat, all-you-can-eat subscription model doesn't map well onto the work we're doing. When an agent runs for a long time, uses a lot of compute, calls tools, and reads a huge amount of material, the cost is real and it varies a lot from task to task. We've tried to align pricing with the value of the outcome and the work actually performed, rather than pretending every query costs the same. Honestly, I think the industry is still figuring this out. Users are used to flat subscriptions, and there's a tension between predictability for the customer and sustainability for us. Our bet is that people doing serious research care more about getting a genuinely good result than about shaving a few cents off a query, as long as we're transparent about what they're paying for.

On the technical side, it pushes us toward a few priorities. The first is reliability over long trajectories. A model that's 95% reliable per step sounds great until you chain a hundred steps and the errors compound. So we invest a lot in error recovery, in the agent noticing when it's gone down a wrong path, and in checkpoints where it can verify its own work.

The second is memory and context management. You can't just stuff everything into one context window and hope. You need ways to keep track of what's been learned, what's been ruled out, and what the open questions are, so the system stays coherent hours into a task.

The third is evaluation. Evaluating a long-horizon research process is much harder than grading a single answer. You care about whether the final output is right, but also whether the process was sound and whether a human expert would trust it. Building good evals for that has been one of the most important, and most underrated, parts of the work.

And the last one is the human in the loop. Long-horizon doesn't mean set it and forget it. The best experience lets the person steer at the right moments: review a plan, redirect when priorities change, and dig into the reasoning behind a conclusion. So a lot of our product thinking goes into making that collaboration feel natural rather than like supervising a black box.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core thing I keep coming back to is that real research doesn't happen in a single prompt. It happens over hours, days, sometimes weeks. You form a hypothesis, you test it, it fails in some interesting way, you revise, you go read three more papers, you talk to someone who tells you your framing is wrong, and you start over. That loop is the actual unit of work, not the individual query. And once you take that seriously, a lot of decisions at Silico fall out almost automatically.

On the pricing side, it means we really don't want to charge per token or per call in a way that makes people flinch every time the agent wants to go deeper. If a researcher is thinking, "I'd love to let this thing run a sweep over fifty candidate approaches, but that's going to cost me a lot," then we've put the incentive in exactly the wrong place. We want the economics to reward letting the system run long. So we've leaned toward pricing that's tied to outcomes and sustained usage, more like you're paying for a collaborator's time over a project, rather than metering every thought. Honestly, it's less about the exact number and more about not creating psychological friction around persistence.

Technically, the long-horizon framing changes what we optimize for. A model that's brilliant on a benchmark but drifts off course after twenty steps is not that useful to us. So we spend a disproportionate amount of effort on memory, on state management, on the agent being able to check its own work and notice when it's gone down a dead end. Verification is a huge part of it. If you're going to run for a long time without a human in the loop, you have to be really good at catching your own mistakes, because errors compound. A small misread of an experimental result at hour two can poison everything after it.

The other piece is tooling. Long-horizon research means the agent needs to actually run code, actually read the literature, actually manage experiments, and come back with artifacts, not just prose. So we prioritize robust execution environments and reproducibility over, say, making the chat interface prettier. And we think a lot about handoffs, because the researcher isn't going to watch the whole thing. They need to be able to come back after a day and quickly understand what was tried, what worked, what didn't, and why. That legibility is a first-class product requirement for us, not a nice-to-have.

So in short, if you believe research is a long game, you build for endurance, self-correction, and trust, and you price it so people aren't afraid to let it keep going.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that research isn’t really a single question and a single answer. You start with a question, you find something surprising, you revise your hypothesis, and that determines what you do next. The value comes from that whole process, which can take a long time.

So from a pricing perspective, you want to support that iteration. If people are thinking about the cost every time they ask a follow-up question, you’re creating friction in exactly the behavior you want to enable. At the same time, a long-running research task can consume a lot of compute, so you have to make the economics sustainable.

Technically, that pushes you toward continuity: maintaining context, tracking what’s been tried, keeping evidence connected to conclusions, and letting the researcher steer as the work evolves. A really impressive answer in one interaction is useful, but the bigger challenge is whether the system can keep making progress across many interactions without losing the thread. That’s the lens I’d use for both pricing and technical priorities: does this help someone carry a research question through to a result they can actually trust?

sol-6.1.text:
I think research is fundamentally a long-horizon task. You’re not necessarily getting value from any single answer; you’re getting value from a process that reduces uncertainty over time. So we want Silico’s pricing to support that process—to make it practical to explore, try things that don’t work, and come back with a better question, without feeling like every interaction has to pay for itself immediately.

Technically, that pushes us toward continuity. Can the system maintain the context of a project, keep track of what it has tried, and use those results to decide what to do next? Can it check its work and recognize when it needs more evidence? A really impressive response in one interaction is useful, but the bigger goal is a system that can make sustained progress on a research problem. The pricing and the engineering priorities need to support that same behavior.
